Franz Boas. The anthropologist who fundamentally reshaped the discipline by championing rigorous fieldwork, cultural relativism, and the rejection of racial hierarchies.

Boas rejected the biological determinism and racial hierarchies that were prevalent in nineteenth-century anthropology. Through his skull measurements, he demonstrated a striking finding: physical variation within racial groups actually exceeded the variation between them. This meant that many of the supposedly fundamental differences between races were illusory.

He pioneered a completely new way of doing anthropology. Rather than engaging in armchair speculation from libraries and studies, Boas insisted on systematic ethnographic fieldwork. He spent years living with the Kwakwaka'wakw peoples of the Pacific Northwest, conducting participant observation in a way that became the standard for modern anthropology.

He advanced the principle of cultural relativism — the idea that cultures must be understood on their own terms rather than judged by the observer's standards. This transformed how anthropologists approach non-Western societies. He established the American anthropology program at Columbia University in 1896, where he mentored an entire generation of foundational figures, including Margaret Mead, Ruth Benedict, and Alfred Kroeber. These students would become the discipline's backbone.

Beyond the classroom, Boas challenged Social Darwinism and polygenesism with data, contributing significantly to mid-twentieth-century anti-racist scholarship and the UNESCO Statement on Race in 1950. He also developed the four-field approach that unified physical anthropology, cultural anthropology, archaeology, and linguistics under one discipline. This model is still used in American universities today.
